newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Rugby Union - All Blacks turn attention to Wallabies.
newsitem.headline: Rugby Union - All Blacks turn attention to Wallabies.

text.p: HAMILTON, June 30 NZPA - As All Blacks turned their focus towards the Bledisloe Cup match against Australia this Saturday, coach John Hart was lamenting the unsuitable leadup to the year's tougher tests after playing matches against Fiji and Argentina.
To counter that next season, The All Blacks' leadup to next year's Bledisloe Cup and Tri-series will include a twin test series at home against England, NZPA reports.
"When we set the schedule, we thought they would be very, very competitive," Hart said of the Pumas after cleaning up the series 2-0 -- 93-8 and 62-10.
"We saw their game at Twickenham (against England in December) and they should have won it."
Hart revealed that two home tests at this time next year against England may avoid any anxiety he and his players were facing in the Bledisloe Cup week.
Argentina, like Fiji, barely raised a sweat inside the All Black jerseys in terms of test rugby.

Though they put up a fight in the second test on Saturday night in Hamilton and stretched the offside law to the limit for that purpose, the All Blacks still had too much all-round play, winning nine tries to one.
"The preparation has been less than desirable," Hart said of Saturday's first Bledisloe Cup match against the Wallabies at Lancaster Park.

"That was probably our disappointment, so that puts a lot of pressure on us in terms of going into next week's preparations, particularly with the Australians coming off two good wins against arguably the best of the northern hemisphere sides (France)."

The positive side to the three easy tests, which produced 34 All Blacks tries to one against in each game, was the emergence of his squad unscathed while Australia's attrition rate increased to include David Wilson and Jason Little, added to the likes of Matthew Burke.
Andrew Mehrtens was yesterday slotted back at first five-eighth in place of Carlos Spencer for Saturday's match in the only change to the starting 15 that won against the Pumas.
Mehrtens strained a hamstring against Fiji and was rested. Alama Ieremia has also been drawn into the frame with his selection in the expanded reserves list.
However, the acid test is likely to go to the pack when the All Blacks assemble in Christchurch tomorrow.
As in the All Black trials, the front five appeared to channel their energies in forward play individually against the Pumas.
That made it easier for their streetwise opponents to get among them and spoil any momentum and continuity that were forming.

Even around the edges, players like Pedro Sporleder, Pablo Camerlinck, Robert Grau and Rolando Martin rammed in either too early or hung in which prompted Hart to remark: "I think there's a new definition for the offside law sometimes."
The Pumas were determined to prevent the All Black frolic a week earlier at Athletic Park. They tackled with conviction, busted in where the All Blacks were loose and never stopped tries.
Nevertheless, they lacked a genuine international dimension to their play.
The All Blacks pinned the tourists in their half for the first 13 minutes before flanker Taine Randell scored.

In all, the All Blacks scored nine tries with Lee Stensness cutting through for his, Tana Umaga finishing a brilliant backline move, as did Carlos Spencer, and prop Mark Allen, a replacement, romping 20 metres at top speed after taking an inside pass from halfback Justin Marshall.

But the flat Pumas defence, led by second five-eighth and captain Lisandro Arbizu, denied the explosive All Black backline time and space to display their full range of individual skills and collective ability before the paying 28,000, as they did in
Wellington a week earlier.
